anchors.quote:
Government, forms of. [_The classification of forms of government which
Plato adopts in the Republic is not exactly the same with that given in
the Statesman or the Laws. Both in the Republic_ {352} _and the Statesman
the series commences with the perfect state, which may be either monarchy
or aristocracy, accordingly as the 'one best man' bears rule or many who
are all 'perfect in virtue'_ [_cp._ Arist. Pol. iv. 2, § 1]. _But in the
Republic the further succession is somewhat fancifully connected with the
divisions of the soul. The rule of reason_ [_i.e. the perfect state_]
_passes into timocracy, in which the 'spirited element' is predominant_
(8. 548), _timocracy into three governments in turn, which represent the
'appetitive principle,'--first, oligarchy, in which the desire of wealth
is supreme_ (8. 533 D; 9. 581); _secondly, democracy, characterised by an
unbounded lust for freedom_ (9. 561); _thirdly, tyranny, in which all evil
desires grow unchecked, and the tyrant becomes 'the waking reality of what
he once was in his dreams only'_ (9. 574 E). _Each of these inferior forms
is illustrated in the individual who corresponds to the state and 'is set
over against it'_ (8. 550 C). _In the Statesman, after the government of
the one or many good has been separated, the remaining forms are
classified accordingly as the government has or has not regard to law, and
democracy is said to be_ (303 A) _'the worst of lawful and the best of
lawless governments'_ (_an expression criticised by Aristotle,_ Pol. iv.
2, § 3). _In the Laws again the subject is differently treated: monarchy
and democracy are described as 'the two mother forms,' which must be
combined in order to produce a good state_ (3. 693), _and the Spartan and
Cretan constitutions are therefore praised as polities in which every form
of government is represented_ (4. 712). _But the majority of existing
states are mere class governments and have no regard to virtue_ (12.
962 E). _These various ideas are nearly all reproduced or criticised in the
Politics of Aristotle, who, however, does not employ the term 'timocracy,'
and adds one great original conception,--the_ [Greek: mesê\ politei/a],
_or government of

anchors.quote:
Idea. [_The Idea of Good is an abstraction, which, under that name at
least, does not elsewhere occur in Plato's writings. But it is probably
not essentially different from another abstraction, 'the true being of
things,' which is mentioned in many of his Dialogues_ [_cp. passages cited
s. v. Being_]. _He has nowhere given an explanation of his meaning, not
because he was 'regardless whether we understood him or not,' but rather,
perhaps, because he was himself unable to state in precise terms the ideal
which floated before his mind. He belonged to an age in which men felt too
strongly the first pleasure of metaphysical speculation to be able to
estimate the true value of the ideas which they conceived_ (_cp. his own
picture of the effect of dialectic on the youthful mind,_ 7. 539). _To
him, as to the Schoolmen of the Middle Ages, an abstraction seemed truer
than a fact: he was impatient to shake off the shackles of sense and rise
into the purer atmosphere of ideas. Yet in the allegory of the cave_
(_Book VII_), _whose inhabitants must go up to the light of perfect
knowledge but descend again into the obscurity of opinion, he has shown
that he was not unaware of the necessity of finding a firm starting-point
for these flights of metaphysical imagination_ (_cp._ 6. 510). _A passage
in the Philebus_ (65 A) _gives perhaps the best insight into his meaning:
'If we are not able to hunt the good with one idea only, with three we may
take our prey,--Beauty, Symmetry, Truth.' The three were inseparable to
the Greek mind, and no conception of perfection could be formed in which
they did not unite._ (Cp. Introduction, pp. lxix, xcvii).]

triumphant demonstration of the superior happiness enjoyed by the just
man. In the First Book several definitions of justice are attempted, all
of which prove inadequate. Glaucon and Adeimantus then intervene:--mankind
regard justice as a necessity, not as a good in itself, or at best as only
to be practised because of the temporal benefits which flow from it: can
Socrates prove that it belongs to a higher class of goods? Socrates in
reply proposes to construct an ideal state in which justice will be more
easily recognised than in the individual. Justice is thus discovered to be
the essential virtue of the state,_ (_a thesis afterwards enlarged upon by
Aristotle_ [Pol. i. 2, § 16; iii. 13, § 3]), _the bond of the social
organization, and, like temperance in the Laws_ [3. 696, 697; 4. 709 E],
_rather the accompaniment or condition of the virtues than a virtue in
itself_ [_cp._ Introduction, p. lxiii]. _Expressed in an outward or
political form it becomes the great principle which has been already
enunciated_ (i. 322), _'that every man shall do his own work;' on this
Plato bases the necessity of the division into classes which underlies the
whole fabric of the ideal state_ (4. 433 foll.; Tim. 17 C). _Thus we are
led to acknowledge the happiness of the just; for he alone reflects in
himself this vital principle of the state_ (4. 445). _The final proof is
supplied by a comparison of the perfect state with actual forms of
government. These, like the individuals who correspond to them, become
more and more miserable as they recede further from the ideal, and the
climax is reached_ (9. 587) _when the tyrant is shown by the aid of
arithmetic to have '729 times less pleasure than the king'_ [_i.e. the
perfectly just ruler_]. _Lastly, the happiness of the just is proved to_
{359} _extend also into the next world, where men appear before the
judgment seat of heaven and receive the due reward of their deeds in this
life._]

Music. [_Music to the ancients had a far wider significance than to us. It
was opposed to gymnastic as 'mental' to 'bodily' training, and included
equally reading and writing, mathematics, harmony, poetry, and music
strictly speaking: drawing, as Aristotle tells us_ (Pol. viii. 3, § 1),
_was sometimes made a separate division._ I. _Music_ (_in this wider
sense_), _Plato says, should precede gymnastic; and, according to a
remarkable passage in the Protagoras_ (325 C), _the pupils in a Greek
school were actually instructed in reading and writing, made to learn
poetry by heart, and taught to play on the lyre, before they went to the
gymnasium. The ages at which children should commence these various studies
are not stated in the Republic; but in the VIIth Book of the Laws, where
the subject is treated more in detail, the children begin going to school
at ten, and spend three years in learning to read and write, and another
three years in music_ (Laws 7. 810). _This agrees very fairly with the
selection of the_ {363} _most promising youth at the age of twenty_ (Rep.
7. 537), _as it would allow a corresponding period of three years for
gymnastic training._ II. _Music, strictly so called, plays a great part in
Plato's scheme of education. He hopes by its aid to make the lives of his
youthful scholars harmonious and gracious, and to implant in their souls
true conceptions of good and evil. Music is a gift of the Gods to men, and
was never intended, 'as the many foolishly and blasphemously suppose,'
merely to give us an idle pleasure_ (Tim. 47 E; Laws 2. 654, 658 E; 7.
802 D). _Neither should a freeman aim at attaining perfect execution_
[_cp._ Arist. Pol. viii. 6, §§ 7, 15]: _in the Laws_ (7. 810) _we are told
that every one must go through the three years course of music, 'neither
more nor less, whether he like or whether he dislike the study.' Both
instruments and music are to be of a simple character: in the Republic
only the lyre, the pipe, and the flute are tolerated, and the Dorian and
Phrygian harmonies. No change in the fashions of music is permitted; for
where there is licence in music there will be anarchy in the state. In
this desire for simplicity and

anchors.quote:
Poetry. [_The Republic is the first of Plato's works in which he seriously
examines the value of poetry in education, and the place of the poets in
the state. The question could hardly be neglected by the philosopher who
proposed to construct an ideal polity or government of the best. For
poetry played a great part in Hellenic life: the children learned whole
poems by heart in their schools_ (Protag. 326 A; Laws 7. 810 C); _the
rhapsode delighted the crowds at the festivals_ (Ion 535); _the theatres
were free, or almost free, to all, 'costing but a drachma at the most'_
(Apol. 26 D); _the intervals of a banquet were filled up by conversation
about the poets_ (Protag. 347 C). _The quarrel between philosophy and
poetry was an ancient one, which had found its first expression in the
attacks of Xenophanes_ (538 B.C.) _and Heracleitus_ (508 B.C.) _upon the
popular mythology. In the earlier dialogues of Plato the poets are treated
with an ironical courtesy, through which an antagonistic spirit is allowed
here and there to appear: they are 'winged and holy beings'_ (Ion 534)
_who sing by inspiration,_ {367} _but at the same time are the worst
possible critics of their own writings and the most self-conceited of
mortals_ (Apol. 22 D). _In the Republic_ (_II and III_), _Plato begins the
trial of poetry by the enquiry whether the tales and legends related by
the epic and tragic poets are true in themselves or likely to furnish good
examples to his future citizens. They cannot be true, for they are
contrary to the nature of God_ (_see s. v._ God), _and they are certainly
not proper lessons for youth. There must be a censorship of poetry, and
all objectionable passages expunged; suitable rules and regulations will
be laid down, and to these the poets must conform. In the Xth Book the
argument takes a deeper tone. The Poet is proved to be an impostor thrice
removed from the truth, a wizard who steals the hearts of the unwary by
his spells and enchantments. Men easily fall into the habit of imitating
what they admire; and the lamentations and woes of the tragic hero and the
unseemly buffoonery of the comedian are equally bad models for the
citizens of a free and noble state.

anchors.quote:
Soul. [_The psychology of the Republic, while agreeing generally with that
of the other Dialogues, is in some respects a modification or developement
of their conclusions.--The division of the soul into three elements,
reason, spirit, appetite, here first assumes a precise form, and
henceforward has a permanent place in the language of philosophy_ (_cp._
Introd. p. lxvii). _On this division the distinction between forms of
government is based_ (_see s. v._ Government). _Virtue, again, is the
harmony or accord of the different elements, when the dictates of reason
are enforced by passion against the appetites, while vice is the anarchy
or discord of the soul when passion and appetite join in rebellion against
reason_ (_cp._ 4. 444; 10. 609 foll.; Soph. 228; Pol. 296 D; Laws 10. 906
C].--_Regarded from the intellectual side the soul is analysed into four
faculties, reason, understanding, faith, knowledge of shadows. These
severally correspond to the four divisions of knowledge_ (6. 511 E), _two
for intellect and two for opinion; and thus arises the Platonic
'proportion,'_--_being_ : _becoming_ :: _intellect_ : _opinion, and
science_ : _belief_ {372} :: _understanding_ : _knowledge of shadows.
These divisions are partly real, partly formed by a logical process,
which, as in so many distinctions of ancient philosophers, has outrun
fact, and are further illustrated and explained by the allegory of the
cave in Book VII_ (_see_ Introduction, p. xciv).--_The pre-existence and
the immortality of the soul are assumed. The doctrine of [Greek:
a)na/mnêsis] or 'remembrance of a previous birth' is not so much dwelt
upon as in the Meno, Phaedo, or Phaedrus, neither is it made a proof of
immortality_ (Meno 86; Phaedo 73). _It is apparently alluded to in the
story of Er, where we are told that 'the pilgrims drank the waters of
Unmindfulness; the foolish took too deep a draught, but the wise were more
moderate'_ (10. 621 A). _In the Xth Book Glaucon is supposed to receive
with amazement Socrates' confident assertion of immortality, although a
previous allusion to another state of existence has passed unheeded_ (6.
498 D); _and in earlier parts of the discussion_ (_e.g._ 2. 362;
anchors.prefix:
27 E, 533 D, 540 A;--five forms of the state and
soul, 4. 445; 5. 449; 9. 577.

anchors.quote:
3. 386),
_the censure which is passed on the common representations of Hades
implies in itself some belief in a future life_ [_cp._ Introduction to
Phaedo, Vol. I]. _The argument for the immortality of the soul is not
drawn out at great length or with the emphasis of the Phaedo. It is
chiefly of a verbal character:--All things which perish are destroyed by
some inherent evil; but the soul is not destroyed by sin, which is the
evil proper to her, and must therefore be immortal_ (_cp._ Introd. p.
clxvi).--_The condition of the soul after death is represented by Plato in
his favourite form of a myth_ [_cp._ Meno 81; Phaedo 88; Gorg. 522]. _The
Pamphylian warrior Er, who is supposed to have died in battle, revives
when placed on the funeral pyre and relates his experiences in the other
world. He tells how the just are rewarded and the wicked punished, and is
privileged to describe the spectacle which he had witnessed of the choice
of a new life by the pilgrim souls. The reward of release from bodily
existence is not held out to the philosopher_ (Phaedo 114 C), _but his
wisdom, which has a deeper root than habit_ (10. 619), _preserves him from
overhaste in his choice and ensures him a happy destiny.--The
transmigration of souls is represented in the myth much as in the Phaedrus
and Timaeus. Plato in all likelihood derived the doctrine from an Oriental
source, but through Pythagorean channels. It probably had a real hold on
his mind, as it agreed, or could be made to agree, with the conviction,
which he elsewhere expresses, of the remedial nature of punishment_ [_cp._
Protag. 323; Gorg. 523-525].

anchors.quote:
State. [_The polity of which Plato 'sketches the outline' in the Republic
may be analysed into two principal elements,_ I, _an Hellenic state of the
older or Spartan type, with some traits borrowed from Athens,_ II, _an
ideal city in which the citizens have all things in common, and the
government is carried on by a class of philosopher rulers who are selected
by merit. These two elements are not perfectly combined; and, as Aristotle
complains_ (Pol. ii. 5, § 18), _very much is left ill-defined and
uncertain._--I. _Like Hellenic cities in general, the number of the
citizens is not to be great. The size of the state is limited by the
requirement that 'it shall not be larger or smaller than is consistent
with unity.'_ [_The 'convenient number' 5040, which is_ {374} _suggested
in the Laws_ (v. 737), _is regarded by Aristotle_ (Pol. ii. 6, § 6) _as an
'enormous multitude.'_] _Again, the individual is subordinate to the
state. When Adeimantus complains of the hard life which the citizens will
lead, 'like mercenaries in a garrison'_ (4. 419), _he is answered by
Socrates that if the happiness of the whole is secured, the happiness of
the parts will inevitably follow. Once more, war is supposed to be the
normal condition of the state, and military service is imposed upon all.
The profession of arms is the only one in which the citizen may properly
engage. Trade is regarded as dishonourable:--'those who are good for
nothing else sit in the Agora buying and selling'_ (2. 371 D); _the
warrior can spare no time for such an employment_ (_ib._ 374 C). [_In the
Laws Plato's ideas enlarge; he thinks that peace is to be preferred to
war_ (1. 628); _and he speculates on the possibility of redeeming trade
from reproach by compelling some of the best citizens to open a shop or
keep a tavern_ (11. 918).]--_In these respects, as well as in the
introduction of common meals, Plato was probably influenced by the
traditional ideal of Sparta_ [_cp._ Introd. p. clxx]. _The Athenian
element appears in the intellectual training of the citizens, and
generally in the atmosphere of grace and refinement which they are to
breathe_ (_see s. v._ Art). _The restless energy of the Athenian

is perhaps reflected in the discipline imposed upon the ruling class_
(7. 540), _who when they have reached fifty are dispensed from continuous
public service, but must then devote themselves to abstract study, and
also be willing to take their turn when necessary at the helm of state_
[_cp._ Laws 7. 807; Thucyd. i. 70; ii. 40].--II. _The most peculiar
features of Plato's state are_ (1) _the community of property,_ (2) _the
position of women,_ (3) _the government of philosophers._ (1) _The first_
(_see s. v._), _though suggested in some measure by the example of Sparta
or Crete_ [_cp._ Arist. Pol. ii. 5, § 6], _is not known to have been
actually practised anywhere in Hellas, unless possibly among such a body
as the Pythagorean brotherhood._ (2) _Nothing in all the Republic was
probably stranger to his contemporaries than the place which Plato assigns
to women in the state. The community of wives and children, though
carefully guarded by him from the charge of licentiousness_ (5. 458 E),
_would appear worse in Athenian eyes than the traditional 'licence' of the
Spartan women_ [Arist. Pol. ii. 9, § 5), _which, so far as it really
existed, no doubt arose out of an excessive regard to physical
considerations in marriage. Again, the equal share in education, in war,
and in administration which the women are supposed to enjoy in Plato's
state, was, if not so revolting, quite as contrary to common Hellenic
sentiment_ [_cp._ Thucyd. ii. 45]. _The Spartan women exercised a great
influence on public affairs, but this was mainly indirect_ [_cp._ Laws 7.
806; Arist. Pol. ii. 9, § 8]; _they did not hold office or learn the use
of arms. At Athens, as is well known, the women, of the upper classes at
least, lived in an almost Oriental seclusion, and were wholly absorbed in
household duties_ (Laws 7. 805 E). (3) _Finally, the government of
philosophers had no analogy in the Hellenic world of_ {375} _Plato's time.
He may have taken the suggestion from the stories of the Pythagorean rule

territories.label: Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia

evidence.rationale: Book I moves through successive definitions of justice (Cephalus's truth-telling and debt-paying, Polemarchus's helping friends/harming enemies, Thrasymachus's interest-of-the-stronger) with refutations culminating in the end–excellence account of the soul and the claim that injustice never profits more than justice, yet ends without ever stating what justice is. Book II renews the charge from a different motive, Glaucon and Adeimantus asking that justice be praised in its effect on the soul and proved good in itself, and only in Book IV is justice claimed to be each part doing its own work in city and soul—including the editorial objection that justice and temperance blur. The whole design thus repeatedly tests whether justice is definable apart from reward or reputation, and the sequence is best read as one connected argument with unresolved points rather than four separate topics. Coverage is the fraction of retained occurrences, not source text. Theme distance is navigational.

territories.label: The city-first method and the State–soul analogy: an indirect answer and a method that is contested even by its own editor

evidence.rationale: Because justice is hard to see in the individual, Socrates enlarges it to the city and reads it back down through an analogy the introduction itself calls fallacious yet fruitful. The building sequence—from exchange-driven specialization to the healthy city, luxury, war and guardians, up to the whole's happiness overriding any class and to each class doing its own work—supports the indirect answer, and the later books deliberately pair each constitution with a character-type to settle the happiness question. The method both structures the work and attracts repeated criticism about the subordination of the individual to the State. Coverage is the fraction of retained occurrences, not source text. Theme distance is navigational.

territories.label: Forming character by nurture: music, gymnastics, restricted stories, and the limits of law

evidence.rationale: Books II–IV argue that guardians are shaped before reason arrives: musical and literary education precedes gymnastic, myth and imitation are censored under theological canons (God causes good only, is changeless, cannot lie), lies are classed as remedies the state monopolizes against the 'lie of the soul', and simpleness of regimen extends to medicine and diet. Music and gymnastics are finally described as two arts tuning the soul's principles under a harmonist, and Book IV subordinates legislation to education and long cultural stability. The introduction's corrections (faculty mapping, the innocence requirement for judges, contested by an editorial note) register disputes within this material. Coverage is the fraction of retained occurrences, not source text. Theme distance is navigational.

territories.label: The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods

evidence.rationale: Book V's three waves extend 'own work' to women guardians by limiting difference of nature to work-relevant differences, then subject mating, rearing, nominal kinship and possessions to the goal of civic unity, answering the possessive-'mine' conflict by shared pleasures and pains. Each wave is literally staged as meeting an objection, and the surrounding commentary splits sharply: Plato's proposals are credited as 'paradoxical' measures toward unity while the editor's historical speculation about property and moral critique of the marriage scheme oppose the scheme's premises. These opposing appraisals belong to one discussion cluster but must be kept as separate occurrences. Coverage is the fraction of retained occurrences, not source text. Theme distance is navigational.

territories.label: From sight to being: the philosopher, the ascent, and the idea of Good as the summit of education

evidence.rationale: Knowledge of unchangeable ideas versus opinion about particulars separates true philosophers from lovers of sights and grounds the claim that only the philosophical nature may govern, answered by the ship parable and a story of philosophy corrupted by public opinion and of the few who withdraw. The sun analogy, the divided line, and the cave allegory stage a hierarchy of four faculties and an ascent above hypotheses; the mathematical curriculum is a prelude whose value lies in abstract problems, with dialectic reaching the first principle and the idea of good. Parallel strands in the sections give opposed verdicts: education as turning and the rulers' duty to descend, versus editorial charges of abstractionism, mis-timed education, and an empty ideal that nonetheless orients inquiry. Coverage is the fraction of retained occurrences, not source text. Theme distance is navigational.

territories.label: Declining constitutions, the tyrannical life, and the grading of pleasure and happiness

evidence.rationale: Books VIII–X pair four defective constitutions with four character-types in decline—timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, tyranny—and use that pairing to answer Thrasymachus about which life is happier. Democratic license is traced through a pleasure taxonomy into tyranny, and the tyrannical man is judged miserable by further arguments: the ranking of five bands, the tripartite soul's pleasures, and the claim that reason-guided pleasures are truer, with the tyrant measured enormously far from them. A separate later commentary questions both the historical fit of the sequence and the seriousness of the Platonic/State number, and the editor deflates the number riddle in reconstructing the 729 cube—so descriptive and critical strands both recur across the sections. Coverage is the fraction of retained occurrences, not source text. Theme distance is navigational.

territories.label: Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states

evidence.rationale: Book X, with the tripartite soul now established, renews the ban on imitative art: makers copy appearances thrice removed and nourish the lower passions unless they plead a civic use. The reply offered in the introduction defends art as mediating feeling and thought and as a possible vehicle of the highest truth—opposed point for point to Plato's objection—while the 'old quarrel' of poetry and philosophy is left open. The closing books prove the soul's immortality from the failure of inherent evil to dissolve it and end in the Myth of Er's judgement, retribution and free choice of lives; the apparatus then reads later ideal states (Rome, Christian city, universal empire, English Utopias) as receptions of Plato and as vehicles for unstatable thought, treating ideals as unrealized visions culminating in the Good. This is generally editorial voice, not endorsed dialogue doctrine, and its uncertainty must be preserved. Coverage is the fraction of retained occurrences, not source text. Theme distance is navigational.

nodes.label: Republic's scope and method
nodes.summary: The commentator calls the Republic Plato's greatest and most wide-ranging work, unique in interweaving life with speculation and politics with philosophy. It is said to contain the germs and first inventions of later logic and psychology (definition, contradiction, essence vs. accidents, division of the soul and of desires) and to insist on the difference between words and things, though Plato himself does not always avoid the confusion, and his logic remains veiled in metaphysics.

evidence.rationale: A sustained evaluative claim about what the work is and what Plato achieved in it. X follows primary theme “The city-first method and the State–soul analogy: an indirect answer and a method that is contested even by its own editor”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Justice's path through the work
nodes.summary: The argument is the search after justice: hinted at by Cephalus, argued on proverbial morality by Socrates and Polemarchus, caricatured by Thrasymachus and partly answered, then abstracted by Glaucon and Adeimantus until justice, invisible in the individual, reappears in the ideal State. From there the treatment moves through education, the higher State ruled by philosopher-kings, the decline through honour-loving government, democracy and tyranny, the resumed quarrel with poetry (poetry as imitation thrice removed from truth, Homer banished), and finally a revelation of a future life.

evidence.rationale: An argument-organizing account linking the dialogue's several movements from first definitions to the afterlife. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Fivefold structure; opposed halves
nodes.summary: The division into books is judged later than Plato; five natural divisions are proposed (introductory refutation of popular justice; construction of the first State and education; Books V–VII, where philosophy and a communist State ruled by philosophers replace justice as the question; the decline of States and of men; the conclusion on poetry and the afterlife). A broader split into Books I–IV (Hellenic religion and morality) and V–X (an ideal kingdom of philosophy) yields two really opposed points of view, making the Republic an imperfect whole; whether this reflects an enlarged plan, unresolved conflicting ideas, or composition at different times cannot be settled.

evidence.rationale: A framework that maps the organization of the dialogue as a whole. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Justice and State as one truth
nodes.summary: Answering Morgenstern and others on whether defining justice or constructing the State is the work's principal argument, the commentator answers that the two blend in one and are two faces of the same truth: justice is the order of the State, the State the visible embodiment of justice in human society — soul and body of one ideal. Justice then reappears throughout the work as the inner law of the soul and as the principle of rewards and punishments in another life, and rests ultimately on the idea of good.

evidence.rationale: A reusable concept equating the work's ethical and political subjects as aspects of one order. X follows primary theme “The city-first method and the State–soul analogy: an indirect answer and a method that is contested even by its own editor”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. nodes.label: Against a single design
nodes.summary: The commentator warns that too much is made of referring every work to a single design: plans grow under an author's hand, and one may as well speak of many designs as one. On this reading the State is a vehicle for several great truths (the idea of good as divine perfection, justice as human perfection, lifelong education, false teachers and evil rulers, a kingdom laid up in heaven), freely mixing ideas, myths, figures and facts; its practicability is therefore irrelevant to its truth. Still, justice is said to bear greater marks of design than the State's framework, and Books V–VII the summit of speculation.

evidence.rationale: An argument about how to read the work that organizes several claims about truth, myth and unity. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Characters as moral stages
nodes.summary: Plato's interlocutors are said to represent successive stages of morality: the old Athenian gentleman Cephalus (who raises justice while resting secure in honest dealing) gives way to the proverbial morality of Polemarchus, then the Sophists' wild generalization in Thrasymachus (Plato's caricature of a celebrated man), and finally the young disciples Glaucon and Adeimantus. These last are distinct rather than doubled roles: Glaucon is vivid, humorous and imaginative and takes the lighter passages, Adeimantus graver and more argumentative, holding Socrates to explanations of women and children, happiness, and the corruption of philosophy.

evidence.rationale: A reusable pattern in which dramatis personae encode a moral and dialectical progression. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Socrates' shifting portrayal

The Socratic method is retained in form but has become a method of teaching through interlocutors who look at a thesis from several points of view.

nodes.label: Ideal happiness and caveats
nodes.summary: Commentary says the two brothers ask Socrates to prove the just happy once everything ordinarily counted as happiness is taken away. It defends such an attempt: every ideal is paradoxical beside ordinary conditions of life and is rarely realized, though a few exceptional individuals may have happiness in death and misery. It adds that Plato is dramatizing one aspect of ethical truth in a series of positions rather than stating his own final conclusion, and that 'happiness' should not be read as the modern notion of conscious pleasure or satisfaction.

evidence.rationale: A reusable concept about the status of ethical ideals and the shift of key terms across philosophical traditions. nodes.label: Justice enlarged to social order
nodes.summary: Commentary reports Adeimantus, taking up Glaucon's hint, arguing that mankind values justice only for rewards and reputation — the advantage convention gives to Thrasymachus and Glaucon — while both brothers question whether morality turns on consequences and go past Socrates' position that justice is desirable both for itself and its results. Commentary then proposes that Socrates enlarges the old-fashioned notion of justice into universal order or well-being, first in the State and then the individual, as the ordering principle of the other three virtues, while trying to reconcile an internal account of justice with man's being a social creature.

nodes.label: State precedes the individual
nodes.summary: Commentary says Plato preserves the Greek order of beginning with the State and going on to the individual — the reverse of the modern order of ideas — since early individuals knew no good or evil apart from the law of their country or creed of their church. nodes.label: Luxury, war, and guardians
nodes.summary: Analysis traces how a city grown from needs and divided labour becomes, at Glaucon's demand for comforts, a luxurious city whose extra mouths require seizure of neighbours' land and so produce war and a soldier class. Applying the division of labour to war raises the guardian problem: the guardian must combine gentleness toward friends with fierceness toward enemies. The dog, gentle to friends and fierce to strangers because it judges by knowing and not knowing, supplies the image: guardians must be philosophers or lovers of learning, whence the question of their education.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: God is good: censoring the tales
nodes.summary: In the guardians' education through music and literature, the reports say nursery tales must be censored because children must not learn what they will later unlearn, and Homer and Hesiod tell immoral falsehoods. Two principles govern: God must be represented as the author of good only, not of evil; and with God is no change of form or variableness — God is true, never deceiving by word or sign, so the poets' shape-shifting and lying divine dreams must be suppressed.

nodes.label: Narrative kinds and imitation
nodes.summary: Analysis reports that narrative is of three kinds — simple, imitative, or mixed (the opening of Homer illustrating the mixed kind) — and that guardians should not be imitators at all, since one man cannot play many parts; if they imitate anything it must be the good, for the actor's mask tends to become his face. The descriptive style with little imitation suits a self-respecting man, while the man without self-respect imitates anybody and anything; the complex polyphonic performer is received with respect but told there is no room for his kind in this State.

nodes.label: Tripartite soul, one justice

nodes.summary: Guardians must be naturally able, balanced in mind and body, and young: at twenty the promising are selected to relate the sciences to true being, at thirty those able to abstract enter dialectic for five or six years, then fifteen years of practical service in the den, and at fifty they turn to the idea of good and take turns governing and training successors.

nodes.label: Premature dialectic unmoors the young
nodes.summary: Socrates warns that dialectic can do evil when taken up too early: like a supposititious son rejecting reputed parents, a young man whose received principles are questioned abandons them for pleasure and lawlessness, so philosophy should begin in sobriety around thirty. nodes.label: Five states, five souls
nodes.summary: Resuming after the digression, the analysis recasts the scheme: besides the perfect State, Hellas has four noteworthy constitutions — Lacedaemonian/Cretan (timocratic), oligarchy, democracy, tyranny — with four matching individual natures. nodes.label: Muses' number splits the metals
nodes.summary: In a jesting Muses' answer, the fall of the perfect State is traced to division among rulers caused by a fixed numerical law of human generation: rulers cannot reckon fertile seasons, marriages fail, 'inferior offspring' become rulers, gymnastic displaces music, and the gold/silver and iron/brass races mix and then pull apart over wealth, compromising on private property and enslaving their former fellow-citizens while keeping their warlike character. nodes.speaker: unnamed analyst (Muses' answer quoted)

nodes.label: Timocracy loses philosophy
nodes.summary: Timocracy keeps the ideal's obedience to rulers, common meals and war/gymnastic training, but philosophy is corrupted, war arts prevail over peace arts, wealth is hoarded, and party spirit and ambition become its mark. The matching man is self-asserting, ill-educated yet fond of reading, obedient to rulers, hungry for honour won by arms, and later avaricious: shaped when his mother and the family servant reproach his retiring father, he settles at a middle point between them.

nodes.speaker: unnamed analyst (Adeimantus's reply quoted)

nodes.label: Oligarchy: two cities in one
nodes.summary: Oligarchy arises when gold and silver possession makes riches outweigh virtue and lovers of money replace lovers of honour; political rights are confined by law to the rich. The city becomes two warring nations of rich and poor, guarded by no arms in the poor's hands, breeding drones with and without stings (paupers and rogues) through bad education and bad government. The matching man, frightened when he sees an honour-loving father ruined by informers, enthrones avarice: outwardly respectable, secretly slavish and mean, he hoards and fights with only a fraction of his resources.

evidence.rationale: A pattern claim pairing the oligarchical regime with its money-ruled character type. X follows primary theme “Declining constitutions, the tyrannical life, and the grading of pleasure and happiness”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · unnamed analyst (dialogue reported)
nodes.speaker: unnamed analyst (dialogue reported)

nodes.label: Democracy: pleasing and lawless
nodes.summary: Democracy takes power when the poor — reduced to dronage by usurers and extravagant habits encouraged by the rich — defeat them, kill or exile some, and give equal shares to all. Its life is freedom of speech and each doing what is right in his own eyes, so the city is 'not one but many', a bazaar where anything can be had: a pleasing, lawless, variety-loving government giving equality to equals and unequals alike and neglecting the training of statesmen. The matching man, son of a miserly oligarch, is lured by the drone's honey and wild companions into a battle in the soul that banishes modesty and temperance under renamed vices, then divides his time impartially between necessary and unnecessary pleasures, unable to rank any of them.

evidence.rationale: A pattern claim pairing the democratic regime with its passion-balanced, pleasure-shifting character type. X follows primary theme “Declining constitutions, the tyrannical life, and the grading of pleasure and happiness”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · dialogue · unnamed analyst (dialogue reported)
nodes.speaker: unnamed analyst (dialogue reported)

nodes.label: Tyrant-wolf devours the people
nodes.summary: Tyranny grows out of democracy's exclusive love of freedom: anarchy spreads through the state and households until no citizen will bear any law. From the drones, rich and labouring classes the people raise a protector who, tasting human blood and bribing with debts and land, must 'become a wolf' — taking a bodyguard and standing as full-blown tyrant in the chariot of State. The people find they have nurtured a monster too strong to expel, beaten by the son they raised: liberty that ignores all order and reason passes into the worst servitude.

nodes.label: Symbol, not solution
nodes.summary: The commentary accepts 216 but rejects Donaldson's mapping of the perfect number to the world and the imperfect to the state, his claim that the second harmony is a cube, and his gloss of 'two incommensurables' as 2 and 3 (reading instead two squares on irrational diameters of a side-5 figure). nodes.label: Three pleasures ranked by knowledge
nodes.summary: The second proof gives three kinds of pleasure answering to reason, passion, and desire, each nature praising only its own pleasures. nodes.speaker: Socrates (dialogue), as paraphrased in the analysis

nodes.label: True pleasure, not relief of pain
nodes.summary: The third proof holds that many bodily pleasures are merely reliefs of pain or anticipations of relief and are misperceived (like a man halfway up mistaking the middle region for the top, or the grey for white against black), whereas some pleasures have no antecedent pains. Satisfaction of what has more being and truth (soul, the invariable) is truer than that of the mortal body; bodily pleasures are shadows mixed with contrast, and insatiable appetites leave a 'leaky' vessel (cf. X follows primary theme “Declining constitutions, the tyrannical life, and the grading of pleasure and happiness”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. nodes.label: King–tyrant gap: 729
nodes.summary: The analysis calls the tyrannical man enslaved — the better part of his soul ruled by the worse, poorer and more miserable than any other, and worse still if he becomes a public tyrant — and then numbers the distance to the king: the tyrant's pleasure is a shadow of a shadow (third removed from the oligarch, the oligarch thrice removed from the king), 3×3 cubed = 729, the 'number of a beast' nearly equal to a year's 365×2 days and nights, making the king 729 times happier than the tyrant.

X follows primary theme “Declining constitutions, the tyrannical life, and the grading of pleasure and happiness”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Soul as beast, lion, and man
nodes.summary: Answering the claim that injustice pays if undetected, the analysis images the soul as a many-headed tame-and-wild beast, a lion, and a smaller man under one human skin: injustice feeds the beasts and starves the man, while justice strengthens the man and allies the lion to subdue the many-headed hydras. Vices map onto each element's misuse (intemperance looses the monster; sullenness fattens the lion; flattery turns it into a monkey), and education and law exist to install the ruling principle.

X follows primary theme “Declining constitutions, the tyrannical life, and the grading of pleasure and happiness”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. nodes.label: Editor on Book IX's pleasure theory
nodes.summary: The commentary's closing introduction singles out three points of Book IX — the account of pleasure, the 729 interval, and the pattern in heaven — and judges the pleasure doctrine moderate: each soul-part should have its natural satisfaction, and pleasure is more than the absence of pain (cf. Philebus). Against the Cynics, towards the Epicureans, and since technicalised by Aristotle, it nevertheless rests on ancient illusions — treating a pleasure's transience as proof of unreality, and conflating the permanence of knowledge with a greater and longer-lasting pleasure.

nodes.label: 729: king to tyrant
nodes.summary: The analyst reads the number 729 (the cube of 9, near the days and nights in a year) as Plato's formula for an immeasurable gap between the king and the tyrant, glossing it as one year of tyrannical life equaling about twelve hours of royal life; the steps to the cube are admittedly hard to reconstruct, the intermediate terms being counted as the side of a square.

nodes.label: Pattern in heaven
nodes.summary: Near the close of Republic IX the heavenly pattern replaces the city of philosophers on earth: the vision is now distant, yet also the rule of man's life within the individual, striking a note that prepares for the revealed future life of the following Book while keeping the political ideal realizable in the individual.

nodes.label: Imitation thrice removed
nodes.summary: In the paraphrased Book X, God makes the one bed of nature and the carpenter a second bed, while the painter imitates the carpenter's bed and so is thrice removed from truth, catching only one appearance of a thing; set beside the arts of use and making, imitation has neither science nor true opinion, being only play or sport.

nodes.speaker: Socrates, voiced in the analyst's paraphrase (Glaucon replying)

nodes.label: Poetry vs the better soul
nodes.summary: Since the same object appears differently at different distances or media and only measure and calculation settle the conflict, imitation is allied to the worse faculty and chiefly displays the sorrowful, irrational part of the soul, while reason is not easily displayed to a mixed crowd; the poet therefore paints inferior truth and an inferior part of the soul and is refused authority over the mind.

nodes.speaker: Socrates, voiced in the analyst's paraphrase (Glaucon replying)

nodes.label: Poetry's ban and her apology
nodes.summary: Because poetry feeds grief and coarse merriment until they rule at home, all of it except hymns to the gods and praises of famous men is prohibited, with law and reason rather than pleasure and pain to rule; yet poetry is offered an apology and readmission on condition of proving itself useful as well as delightful, against the acknowledged ancient quarrel between poetry and philosophy and with the soul's good or evil as the stake.

evidence.rationale: a reusable concept: a standing conflict adjudicable by an announced standard. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. nodes.speaker: Socrates, voiced in the analyst's paraphrase; interlocutor agrees

nodes.label: Soul's indestructibility
nodes.summary: Each thing is destroyed only by its own inherent evil; injustice, the soul's proper corruption, does not kill the soul (or criminals would die unaided), and bodily evil cannot destroy what is a different thing — so the soul is immortal and everlasting, of the fairest and simplest composition, seen at present encrusted like the sea-god Glaucus and best viewed in philosophy.

evidence.rationale: a reusable argument-form: failure of internal corruption entails indestructibility. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. nodes.speaker: Socrates, voiced in the analyst's paraphrase (interlocutor objecting and conceding)

nodes.label: Art feeds passion, not reason
nodes.summary: The commentator reports Plato's Tenth Book charge that imitation expresses the emotional rather than the rational part of us and, refusing the Aristotelian purgation of passions, only lets us indulge them; but the commentator grants that voiced feeling can sometimes console and heal what is pent up.

evidence.rationale: A single reported claim about what imitation does to the soul. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Sense-poetry vs idea-philosophy
nodes.summary: Explains the ancient quarrel by allying poetry with particulars of sense and philosophy (Socrates and Plato) with universals and abstraction, noting that Aristotle reverses the valuation by finding poetry, unlike history, concerned with universals (Poetics c. 9, 3).

evidence.rationale: A reusable scheme (sense/particulars against idea/universal) for the conflict between poets and philosophy. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Particulars can also be true
nodes.summary: The commentator argues that Plato's preference for universals is illusory: an individual man or bed is no more erroneous than its class, universals may be false while particulars are true, and Greek ambiguity about opinion and sensation bred Plato's denial of truth to sense-particulars.

evidence.rationale: A general claim about where truth can reside, usable beyond Plato's case. X follows primary theme “From sight to being: the philosopher, the ascent, and the idea of Good as the summit of education”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Poetry in the service of tyranny
nodes.summary: A further count in the indictment: poets, with sophists and rhetoricians, are cast as false teachers and courtiers of tyrants, and the commentator asserts that despotism cannot be maintained without corrupted literature and claims on the imagination of the masses.

evidence.rationale: A political charge asserted about poets and rulers, not a general framework. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Art joins thought and feeling
nodes.summary: Against eradication of the emotions, the commentator holds emotions are neither good nor bad in themselves: art presents thought in the form of feeling and, as a necessary compromise of ideal and exact, stands between sense and ideas; since imagination underlies thought and language, banishing it would be impossible as well as suicidal.

evidence.rationale: A reusable concept of art's mediating function between sense and ideas. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Poetry that serves mankind
nodes.summary: Reading the banishment of the poets as protest against degenerate verse rather than literal exile, the commentator imagines a poetry of divine truth and justice, measures named poets by that standard (with praise for some and fault found with others, including that one 'has left no way of life'), and closes with the question of how the gift of poesy may be devoted to the good of mankind.

evidence.rationale: An argument connecting several criteria (truth, justice, moral effect) by which poetry is judged. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Choice within necessity
nodes.summary: In the analysis of the Myth of Er, chance in the order of lots may be overcome by choosing with wisdom; hibitual goodness is inferior and must add knowledge to act well in new circumstances (the Coleridge parallel is the commentator's), and free will to reject evil is real though bounded by necessity and unequal circumstances.

evidence.rationale: A reusable model of moral agency joining fortune, knowledge and will. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Paradoxes of the perfect State
nodes.summary: Opening the survey, the commentator says Plato's perfect State is full of paradox by ordinary standards: moderns have sneered at its proposals as absurd or immoral or taken comfort in Aristotle's criticisms. But errors with a side of truth, and truths mixed with error (where 'the half is better than the whole'), may still be a contribution to the study of human nature and deserve careful treatment rather than alarm about existing institutions.

evidence.rationale: An argument that sets the terms for the whole ensuing survey of Plato's paradoxical proposals and tells the reader how to weigh them. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction)
nodes.speaker: editorial commentator (Introduction)

nodes.label: Community of goods and critics
nodes.summary: The first paradox is community of goods, mentioned briefly at the end of Book III and, as Aristotle observes, seemingly confined to the guardians — an omission the commentator attributes to the plan of the work rather than to significance. Aristotle censures common property as repressing industry and benevolence, and modern writers treat the question as already settled by mankind's common opinion. Against this the commentator urges that the sacredness of property is far more fixed in modern than in ancient times, when debt, war, revolution and legislation made holdings insecure, and that even early Christians held goods in common.

evidence.rationale: A reusable, contestable institutional scheme — common ownership of goods — capable of opposing assessments across periods. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction)
nodes.speaker: editorial commentator (Introduction)

nodes.label: Equal work and training for women
nodes.summary: Plato prefaces community of wives with a proposal that men and women take the same occupations and training. The apparent clash with the rule that different natures choose different pursuits (and with the division of labour) is answered within his scheme: the only organic difference is that men beget and women bear children, natural gifts being scattered indifferently between the sexes (with at most a difference of degree), and the indecency objection is answered as mere habit. The commentator concedes the modern counter that the differences of sensibility and energy 'affect the whole nature', but holds it unclear how far these are produced by education, inherited custom and mode of life, so that Plato 'may have been right' to admit no ultimate difference beyond that which exists in animals.

evidence.rationale: A reusable claim that sex differences do not warrant different functions in the state, with opposed assessments preserved. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction), reporting and contending with Plato
nodes.speaker: editorial commentator (Introduction), reporting and contending with Plato

nodes.label: Marriage as race-breeding
nodes.summary: The second paradox, community of wives and children, is put as 'Is it possible? Is it desirable?' with Glaucon's doubts and stronger doubts of the commentator's. The commentator first reconstructs Plato's motives: the relations intended are an impossible strictness rather than licence, the family is treated as the natural enemy of the state in hope of an universal brotherhood, and pairing is directed solely to improvement of the race, with only the fitter lives preserved. The same passage then refuses the ideal in the name of Christian care for the weakest — infant, criminal, insane — and the endless value of the individual, so that to a modern and Christian view Plato is 'sanctioning murder and destroying the first principles of morality'.

evidence.rationale: A concept-pattern — regulating human pairing for offspring quality — presented through two opposed evaluations. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction), reporting Plato and Glaucon
nodes.speaker: editorial commentator (Introduction), reporting Plato and Glaucon

nodes.label: Man exceeds the animal analogy
nodes.summary: The commentator argues that the great error of these speculations is forgetting the difference between man and the animals: humans are viewed as by a dog- or bird-fancier, and improvement is taken to be size, flesh and strength, whereas human improvement is the growth of mind — so there must be 'a marriage of true minds', which the scheme destroys along with all parental and conjugal affection, though even the nobler animals (Plato's own illustration) remain faithful and nurse their young. Parallel claim: life should rest on a moral rather than a physical basis, mind caring for both body and mind, with the moral as the expansion of the physical and no health of mind without duty and love of truth.

evidence.rationale: An argument joining several concepts (person, mind and body, moral worth) and thereby grounding the critique of the marriage scheme. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction)
nodes.speaker: editorial commentator (Introduction)

nodes.label: Monogamy and the family defended
nodes.summary: The commentator appeals to history against the Platonic marriage: wherever polygamy prevailed the race deteriorated, 'one man to one woman' has once taken by civilized peoples never been retraced, and close intermarriage tends to weakness in children — evidence that morality asserts its authority in the relations of the sexes. Against recent anthropological inference from primitive tribes he protests that the social record is fragmentary and that monogamous care of young in animals cuts the other way. Yet if marriage grew historically out of barbarian selfishness, its idea has been progressively defined and consecrated (East, Greeks and Romans, Christian nations); that view supplies a firmer reason to hold it sacred, with a warning not to abandon moral principle in the uncertainty of transitional knowledge.

evidence.rationale: A reusable norm — the moral authority of monogamous marriage — argued for historically and against opposing anthropological speculation. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction)
nodes.speaker: editorial commentator (Introduction)

nodes.label: Heredity cannot breed genius
nodes.summary: The closing argument denies that artificial breeding can improve mankind: strength and health are not the only goods, mind and character matter more, and the problem is complex (four generations back yield some thirty progenitors) while true inheritance of genius cannot be distinguished from imitation and circumstance. Great men and women have rarely had great parents, and the descendants of the English poets are undistinguished, so the fancy that matched pairings could produce a Shakespeare or Milton is ridiculed. Many of the noblest were physically weak (Tyrtaeus, Aesop, Newton), and mankind passed from brutal to civilized marriage not by pairing strong with strong or dissimilar natures, but by other means.

evidence.rationale: A linked set of claims about the limits of heredity as an instrument of human improvement. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · editorial commentator (Introduction)
nodes.speaker: editorial commentator (Introduction)

nodes.label: Heredity limited by the will
nodes.summary: Editorial argument: inherited mental and physical qualities, popularly noticed in families, can be neither measured nor make up much of a person. Foreknowledge of family disease can guide prevention, so heredity, 'from being a curse, may become a blessing', and within the wall of necessity the will can still 'creat[e] a life for ourselves'.

evidence.rationale: A claim about the limited weight of inheritance and the residuum left to the will. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person)
nodes.speaker: commentary voice (first person)

nodes.label: Family: nurture and cost
nodes.summary: Opposed editorial claims held together: children cannot be reared outside families ('a subtle sympathy between the mother and the child'), so Plato's all-foundling state would mostly perish, 'so emphatically does nature protest against the destruction of the family'; yet family attachments do 'interfere with higher aims', diverting people from country or the ideal, so Plato is credited (though not morally defended) with showing the reverse side of the picture.

evidence.rationale: Paired claim-level evaluations of the family, deliberately kept in tension rather than generalized into one doctrine. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.speaker: commentary voice (first person)

nodes.label: Genius smothered by uniformity
nodes.summary: Editorial claim: Plato misapplied Sparta—Spartan physique owed chiefly to temperance and training, not marriage law; Sparta's fixed laws allowed no individual to rise above the state, and it lacked Athens' greatness (its 'genius... the love of liberty'). Progress in cities and nations comes from remarkable individuals whose origins we cannot control, and systems that extinguish such 'sparks of genius and character' deserve strong condemnation.

evidence.rationale: Reusable concept of the exceptional individual as the source of civic progress, contrasted with state-shaped uniformity. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Population and marital prudence
nodes.summary: Editorial argument: 'Population is the most untameable force in the political and social world'; improvident marriage worsens poverty (large cities, India, Ireland) and generates sickly descendants, yet the passions outrun prudence and wisdom is lost 'just in that action of our lives in which we have the most need of it', so remedies are mainly indirect. Rare individuals (Dr. Combe; a friend wearing a black ribbon as a warning against marriage owing to inherited insanity) did from duty what others should; such marriages ought if possible to be prevented and might come to carry a 'horror naturalis', but law is unenforceable and, the commentary concedes, reason seldom overcomes 'the irresistible impulse of individual attachment'.

evidence.rationale: An argument organizing population pressure, heredity, moral duty, and political impracticability into one assessment of marriage reform. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person), with quoted dramatic line
nodes.speaker: commentary voice (first person), with quoted dramatic line

nodes.label: Plato's all-sufficing State
nodes.summary: Editorial analysis of Plato's political idea: where we see the State as built up from or enclosing family life, Plato treats the family as 'a disturbing influence' against the State's higher unity; no organization but a political (and military) one is needed, and the citizen's whole life is war, preparation for war, and, in old age, philosophy. The commentator finds 'an element of monasticism even in Plato's communism' and notes that the Laws (v. 739 B) does not retract the error, permitting marriage only through 'the infirmity of mankind'.

evidence.rationale: Reusable concept of a State that absorbs all other desires and affections, with a noted monastic analogy. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person), analyzing Plato's position
nodes.speaker: commentary voice (first person), analyzing Plato's position

nodes.label: State/individual fallacy and gain
nodes.summary: Editorial critique balanced by concession: Plato's assimilation of state to individual and confusion of ethics with politics rest on a 'partly fallacious' analogy, since a nation's will is a balance or surplus of interacting individual wills and collective action lacks a single man's pliancy; he also misuses verbal analogies (harmony of sounds to harmony of life), though 'through this fallacious medium, a real enlargement of ideas is attained'. Identifying ethics with politics gave both definiteness and moral elevation, its modern separation has its own losses, and 'when the errors against which they were directed have passed away, they in turn become errors'.

evidence.rationale: An argument weighing a fallacious analogy against the conceptual gains it produced, and tracing the reversal of corrective maxims. X follows primary theme “The city-first method and the State–soul analogy: an indirect answer and a method that is contested even by its own editor”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person)
nodes.speaker: commentary voice (first person)

nodes.label: Education for the whole of life
nodes.summary: Editorial account of Plato's education as partly Greek and partly ideal: he is the first to say education 'is to comprehend the whole of life, and to be a preparation for another in which education begins again (vi. 498 D)'—'the continuous thread' of the Republic and most applicable to modern life. Views have shifted from the Protagoras (virtue teachable; one virtue thesis modified) while Socratic residues remain: education 'implant[s] a principle of intelligence... better than ten thousand eyes', is 'not... the filling of a vessel, but... the turning the eye of the soul towards the light', and 'centre[s] all goodness in the contemplation of the idea of good'. On gymnastic, both music and gymnastic aim at the mind and the lower serves the higher, though strict separation of body and mind training is judged mistaken.

evidence.rationale: Reusable concept of education as lifelong, soul-directing formation, with attendant claims about curriculum and the mind-body training question. X follows primary theme “From sight to being: the philosopher, the ascent, and the idea of Good as the summit of education”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentary voice (first person)
nodes.speaker: commentary voice (first person)

nodes.label: Simplicity in medicine and law
nodes.summary: The commentator reads Plato as urging simplicity in medicine and law alike: modern physicians, gaining in analysis of parts, lose their grasp of the frame as a whole and overcomplicate disease, while in law the greater matters go to the legislator or the oracle of Delphi and the lesser to the citizens themselves. State ills, like hydra heads, are best prevented by care of education rather than extirpated. The commentator also faults Plato's depreciation of diet and his willingness to let invalids die.

evidence.rationale: A claim/pattern attributing one governing norm across two domains. X follows primary theme “Forming character by nurture: music, gymnastics, restricted stories, and the limits of law”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.speaker: commentator (introduction/analysis)

nodes.label: Mathematics trains abstraction
nodes.summary: After the music-and-gymnastic stage, education restarts at a higher level: true knowledge is of universals, and the aim of education is the habit of abstraction, acquired through the mathematical sciences, which give ideas of relation and arouse thought. The commentator notes that in Plato's day mathematics was the mind's only instrument for reducing particulars to rule and order, though Plato already saw that geometrical forms are borrowed from the sensible world.

evidence.rationale: A reusable concept: abstraction as the goal of a stage of education. X follows primary theme “From sight to being: the philosopher, the ascent, and the idea of Good as the summit of education”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. nodes.speaker: commentator (introduction/analysis)

nodes.label: Dialectic above mathematics
nodes.summary: Ideas of number are secondary to a higher conception of knowledge: the dialectician stands above the mathematician as the mathematician above ordinary men, and the self-proving good is the truth to which all things ascend. The commentator presents the idea of good, viewed subjectively, as dialectic (division and collection, definition of essences, piercing hypotheses to the first principle) and says Plato's own dialogues exemplify this method; viewed objectively it is a power or cause aligning the outer and inner world of ideas.

evidence.rationale: An ordering argument joining abstraction, mathematics, dialectic, and the good into a graded epistemology. X follows primary theme “From sight to being: the philosopher, the ascent, and the idea of Good as the summit of education”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.speaker: commentator (introduction/analysis)

nodes.label: The good: vacant yet directive
nodes.summary: The commentator calls the self-proving unity or idea of good 'a mere vision' admitting no distinct explanation, an abstraction comprehending no individuals (a vacancy Aristotle perceived but Plato did not), and argues the dialectical method advanced no further. Yet he adds that such vacant ideals can powerfully direct minds: a true ideal of what knowledge ought to be, unlike a false one such as the scholastic philosophy, presses inquiry forward toward unity, classification, and certainty.

evidence.rationale: A reusable conceptual claim about how contentless ideals orient inquiry. X follows primary theme “From sight to being: the philosopher, the ascent, and the idea of Good as the summit of education”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentator (introduction/analysis)
nodes.speaker: commentator (introduction/analysis)

nodes.label: Education continued through life
nodes.summary: The commentator credits Plato with holding that education continues through life and begins again in another, alongside his delight in the idea of good and solid geometry — but estimates this is the ideal life of the philosopher or genius, for the few, since worldly occupations crowd out study and most people lack the energy and the way to keep improving. He then lists practical counsels for self-education: choose an inclining subject, keep great authors as companions, give an hour a day to enquiry, judge by facts not opinion, and know one's own limits.

evidence.rationale: A reusable concept (self-education across a lifetime) with practical specifications. X follows primary theme “From sight to being: the philosopher, the ascent, and the idea of Good as the summit of education”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentator (introduction/analysis)
nodes.speaker: commentator (introduction/analysis)

nodes.label: Ancients lacked idea of progress
nodes.summary: The commentator observes that Plato and Aristotle seem hardly ever to have considered the regular growth or progress of states and institutions: ancient fixation on divinely sanctioned fundamental law, he suggests, helps explain Plato's intolerance of innovators (though Plato allowed studied foreign improvements and some change short of altering fundamental institutions). Experience gave the Greeks cycles of civilization rather than growth; the idea of progress and of a philosophy of history is modern, fed by Rome, the Church, revolutions, material prosperity, and the study of history, while the small Greek state's vision was 'necessarily limited'.

evidence.rationale: A comparative argument spanning ancient and modern conceptions of historical change. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentator (introduction/analysis)
nodes.speaker: commentator (introduction/analysis)

nodes.label: Ideal republics after Plato
nodes.summary: The commentator claims that writers after Plato likewise used an 'ideal Republic' to carry thoughts they could not express definitely or that outran their age. The nearest classical parallel is Cicero's De Republica, which imitates the Republic's portraits, democracy, tyrant and vision of Er (romanized as the Somnium Scipionis) but falls short in dramatic art and originality while sounding the note of Roman patriotism.

evidence.rationale: A reusable claim about the genre of ideal-state writing, illustrated by Cicero. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary · commentator (introduction/analysis)
nodes.speaker: commentator (introduction/analysis)

nodes.label: Cicero romanizes Plato
nodes.summary: The commentary judges Cicero's De Republica a Roman imitation of Plato: the Somnium Scipionis 'romanizes' Er's vision and adds an immortality argument derived from the Phaedrus, yet remains an inferior dream; the dialogues make speeches rather than converse, and the philosophical writings show no original thinker.

evidence.rationale: A comparative critical claim about how Cicero adapts and falls short of Plato. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset.
