nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Augustine's City of God
nodes.summary: St Augustine's De Civitate Dei, prompted by the fall of Rome as Plato's Republic by the decline of Greek politics, answers the pagan claim that Christianity ruined the empire by blaming pagan vice, tracing sacred and profane history toward a true City of God. The commentary finds the work polemical and wholly uncritical in its use of sources, yet holding passages 'for all time'.

evidence.rationale: A claim evaluating one work's thesis, method, and enduring value. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Dante's De Monarchia
nodes.summary: Dante's De Monarchia presents a universal empire, divinely authorized yet distinct from the Papacy and justified by Roman virtue; its case mixes a priori reasoning with misused Scripture, history, and Aristotle, but is anchored in the misery of the world and the hope that life may pass 'in freedom and peace'. The commentary stresses the vision is inseparable from Dante's own age and beliefs.

evidence.rationale: Summarizes a reusable political ideal: single universal rule as the condition of human peace. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: More's Utopia mirrors England
nodes.summary: More, writing at about 34-35, brings 'the light of Plato' to bear on post-Wars-of-the-Roses England, placing Book One's clerical corruption, luxury, poverty, and war beside the ideal commonwealth of Book Two built with Plato's help and committed to community of property.

evidence.rationale: A claim about the work's design as a critique-and-ideal contrast. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: More's feigned travel narrative
nodes.summary: The commentary credits More's dramatic invention and art of feigning as a Platonic disciple's: he builds on lines of Vespucci, mixes real figures (John Clement, Peter Giles) with the imaginary Hythloday, adds pseudo-documentary disputes and excuses so that the island's location is 'lost with him' and Utopia remains unknown.

evidence.rationale: A pattern claim about the fiction's craft of simulated eyewitness credibility. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Utopia's tolerance, veiled author
nodes.summary: The Utopians exclude unbelievers from office but punish no unbelief and use non-sectarian prayer, which the commentary reads as More exceeding both Plato and his age in tolerance (with a footnote where dissenters are exiled as seditious, not irreligious). Yet More disclaims agreement with all Utopian customs, so the commentary urges keeping the veil over his own voice.

evidence.rationale: An interpretive claim about Utopian religious policy and the text's refusal to disclose More's own view. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Ideals and the Idea of Good
nodes.summary: The closing sections (VII-VIII) argue that ideals, like the examples of great men, raise individuals and states though never directly practicable, remaining 'visions of a world unrealized' with which Plato fixes the mind's eye in the distance. They set beside each other the modern hopes of mankind's future in this world and of individual life beyond it, warn that language's figures must not enslave meditation on God, and name Christ as the human image of that Idea of Good Plato 'saw dimly in the distance'.

evidence.rationale: A closing argument organizing ideals, faith, immortality, and the Idea of Good into one framework. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: Introduction and analysis · commentary

nodes.label: Old age: temper, not years
nodes.summary: Cephalus reports that complaints of old age misattribute their cause: the burdens of age fall on men of ungoverned temper, while a calm nature feels little pressure; he cites Sophocles on escaping a mad master of passion.

evidence.rationale: A claim Cephalus offers from experience and testimony. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.speaker: Cephalus (narrated by Socrates)

nodes.label: Wealth and deathbed conscience
nodes.summary: Prodded by Socrates' suggestion that wealth, not disposition, makes age bearable, Cephalus answers that riches' greatest benefit to a good man is enabling him to avoid wronging others and to face death without fear of unpaid debts or divine penalties—something neither virtue alone nor riches alone secures.

evidence.rationale: A claim about what old age and wealth do, offered as Cephalus's opinion. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Cephalus (narrated by Socrates)
nodes.speaker: Cephalus (narrated by Socrates)

nodes.label: Justice: good to friends, harm to enemies
nodes.summary: After Socrates defeats the formula 'speak truth and pay debts' with the case of a weapon lent to a friend gone mad, Polemarchus inherits the argument and, via Simonides, first says justice is repaying debts, then that it is giving what is proper to each—construed as doing good to friends and evil to enemies, later corrected to those who are really (not merely seemingly) good or bad.

evidence.rationale: A reusable definition of justice proposed and twice revised across the exchange. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Polemarchus (on Simonides; questioned by Socrates)
nodes.speaker: Polemarchus (on Simonides; questioned by Socrates)

nodes.label: The just cannot injure anyone
nodes.summary: Socrates argues that injuring a person worsens him in human virtue, i.e. makes him unjust, and that no art or good produces its own opposite—so harming even a bad enemy cannot be an act of justice, refuting the debt-repayment formula and prompting Polemarchus's agreement.

evidence.rationale: An argument assembling claims about harm, virtue, and arts producing opposites to overturn a rival definition. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates (with Polemarchus assenting)
nodes.speaker: Socrates (with Polemarchus assenting)

nodes.label: Justice is the interest of the stronger
nodes.summary: Abandoning the preceding exchange as folly, Thrasymachus proclaims that justice is nothing other than the interest of the stronger: each regime makes laws for its own advantage and calls obedience to them justice, so universally justice is the interest of the government.

evidence.rationale: A competing general definition of justice applied to all states. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Thrasymachus (narrated by Socrates)
nodes.speaker: Thrasymachus (narrated by Socrates)

nodes.label: Fallible rulers contradict that claim
nodes.summary: Socrates objects that rulers can legislate contrary to their own interest; since subjects must obey, justice on Thrasymachus's showing becomes the injury of the stronger as much as his interest—a conclusion clearest in Socrates' own restatement and granted by Polemarchus.

evidence.rationale: An objection built from premises about obedience, statutory justice, and rulers' error. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates (Polemarchus concurring)
nodes.speaker: Socrates (Polemarchus concurring)

nodes.label: Cleitophon: what rulers think useful
nodes.summary: Cleitophon intervenes with a salvage reading: Thrasymachus meant the interest the stronger merely thinks to be his interest—though Polemarchus denies these were Thrasymachus's words, and Thrasymachus himself rejects the amendment, refusing to call the mistaken a ruler at that moment.

evidence.rationale: A single proposed reinterpretation and its local rejection, not a settled doctrine. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Cleitophon (disputed by Polemarchus and Thrasymachus)
nodes.speaker: Cleitophon (disputed by Polemarchus and Thrasymachus)

nodes.label: No craft erring in respect of itself
nodes.summary: Thrasymachus's second line of defence, preserved here chiefly in an editorial sidenote, is that no artist or ruler errs in so far as he really is what his name implies; his own quoted words deny that one who is mistaken counts as 'stronger' at that moment. The full reply continues beyond the core text supplied.

evidence.rationale: A reusable analytical move: naming a practitioner by the unfailing part of his competence. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Thrasymachus (reply partly preserved in an editorial sidenote)
nodes.speaker: Thrasymachus (reply partly preserved in an editorial sidenote)

nodes.label: Justice = stronger's interest
nodes.summary: In dialogue, Thrasymachus defends 'justice is the interest of the stronger' by a qua-principle: no craftsman, sage, or ruler errs insofar as he is what his name implies (earlier talk of erring practitioners was loose speech), so the ruler qua ruler commands what is for his own interest and the subject must obey.

evidence.rationale: Combines a reusable qua-principle about names and skill with a stated definition of justice, not a single concrete detail. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Thrasymachus, replying to Socrates
nodes.speaker: Thrasymachus, replying to Socrates

nodes.label: Arts serve their subjects
nodes.summary: Socrates argues that an art has no defect of its own to correct and therefore considers only the interest of its subject-matter (medicine serves the body, horsemanship the horse); ruling arts (physician, pilot) therefore prescribe for the subject's good, not the ruler's profit. Thrasymachus gives reluctant assents, reported in the dialogue.

evidence.rationale: A general functional principle about any art and any rule, reusable beyond these examples; borderline claim-level, since it is argued stepwise. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Socrates, with Thrasymachus's reluctant assents
nodes.speaker: Socrates, with Thrasymachus's reluctant assents

nodes.label: Justice is another's good
nodes.summary: Thrasymachus retorts that shepherds and state rulers study their own advantage: justice is in reality another's good, the ruler's interest and the subject's loss, while injustice is one's own profit. He instances partnerships, taxation, office, and above all tyranny, where wholesale fraud and force win happiness and praise.

evidence.rationale: A rival general definition of justice developed through many instances; borderline Y1 as an attributed claim. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.sourceLabel: BOOK I · dialogue · Thrasymachus, in his sustained speech
nodes.speaker: Thrasymachus, in his sustained speech

nodes.label: Art of payment distinguished
nodes.summary: Socrates distinguishes each art's proper function (medicine gives health, navigation safety) from the separate art of payment; a practitioner's gain comes from an added use of the paid art, not from the art he professes, and he benefits his subject even when unpaid.

evidence.rationale: A reusable distinction between an art's function and the benefit of pay that any craft case can instantiate. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.speaker: Socrates, with Thrasymachus's reluc

nodes.label: Injustice as virtue and wisdom
nodes.summary: Socrates expresses amazement that Thrasymachus classes injustice with wisdom and virtue and justice with folly; Thrasymachus explicitly confirms the classification ('Certainly I do so class them'; 'You have guessed most infallibly'), so the dispute is no longer on received principles.

evidence.rationale: An attributed reclassification claim that sharpens the debate but is presented as Thrasymachus's position, not settled doctrine. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Knower does not exceed his like
nodes.summary: Socrates generalizes that a knowledgeable person would claim the same as his like rather than more, while the ignorant desire more than both, and derives that the just (who claims more only of the unjust) resembles the wise and good and the unjust the ignorant — granted repeatedly but with extreme reluctance by Thrasymachus.

evidence.rationale: A general pattern about knowledge and desire to exceed others, applied here to just and unjust; borderline Y1 as a claim of this argument. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.speaker: Socrates, with Thrasymachus's reluctant admissions

nodes.label: Injustice defeats common action
nodes.summary: Socrates argues injustice creates discord and is self-frustrating wherever it dwells: no city, army, family, or even a single person can act in common while unjust, so even successful evil-doers must retain some justice to cooperate. Thrasymachus agrees, at one point declining to oppose the speaker for fear of displeasing the company — a qualification preserved in the dialogue.

evidence.rationale: A pattern claim about injustice's consequences across group and individual cases. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.speaker: Socrates, with Thrasymachus's qualified agreements

nodes.label: Justice as soul's excellence
nodes.summary: The exchange presumes, with agreement, that justice is the excellence of the soul and injustice its defect.

evidence.rationale: A reusable conception of justice as a state of the soul used as a premise. X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Glaucon revives the challenge
nodes.summary: Glaucon, dissatisfied with Thrasymachus's retirement, asks Socrates whether he really persuades that justice always beats injustice, then announces a three-part case: the conventional origin of justice; that it is practised unwillingly and of necessity; and that (against his own view) the reputed argument makes the unjust life out to be better. nodes.summary: Glaucon distinguishes goods prized only for their own sake, goods prized both intrinsically and for results (knowledge, sight, health), and goods only for their results though disagreeable. nodes.label: Justice as compact of the weak
nodes.summary: Reporting the common view, Glaucon says doing injustice is naturally good and suffering it evil; unable to secure the one without the other, men covenant not to do or suffer it, so that legal-and-just is a tolerated middle state, honoured only because men lack power to be unjust.

X follows primary theme “Justice as the governing question: definition, refutation, and lingering aporia”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.summary: Glaucon constructs two ideal types: a perfectly unjust man who is never unjust or found out and keeps the greatest reputation for justice and all its advantages, and a wholly just man who 'wishes to be and not to seem good', is credited with injustice and dies unbenefited; on these extremes judgment of the happier life is to be given.

nodes.label: Adeimantus: praise is for outcomes
nodes.summary: Adeimantus adds that parents, poets (Hesiod, Homer, Musaeus), and prose writers praise justice only for reputation, office, divine gifts and afterlife drink, blame injustice with hell-pains, call vice easy and virtue toilsome, and let sins be expiated by sacrifices and mysteries so the gods can be persuaded. nodes.label: Praise justice in the soul itself
nodes.summary: Adeimantus charges that no panegyrist has shown justice's and injustice's essential nature in the soul, justice being the soul's greatest good and injustice its greatest evil. nodes.label: Luxury leads to war
nodes.summary: Socrates argues that the healthy State must be enlarged with callings answering no natural want (huntings and actors, poets and rhapsodists, cooks, confectioners, etc.) and more physicians; the territory then becomes insufficient, so each city will want a slice of its neighbour's land if it pursues unlimited accumulation of wealth, and war follows — war being derived here from causes said to be behind almost all evils in cities, public and private (Socrates withholds any judgment whether war does good or harm).

nodes.label: One art per man: war
nodes.summary: Applying the earlier principle that one man cannot practise many arts with success, Socrates argues that war is an art demanding as much attention as shoemaking and cannot be left to a farmer or artisan; since nobody becomes a competent player or craftsman at odd moments, and no tool makes an untrained man skilful, the fighting must be done by specialists with natural aptitude, from whom the city's guardians must be selected.

nodes.label: Gentle yet spirited guardians
nodes.summary: Guardians need bodily speed and strength and a soul full of spirit (as in dogs), yet spirited natures tend to be savage; they must be dangerous to enemies and gentle to friends, which seems a contradiction. nodes.label: Music first; tales censored
nodes.summary: Guardians' education follows the traditional two divisions, gymnastic for the body and music for the soul, music (including literature, true and false) coming first because fictitious stories are told to children before gymnastics; since the beginning forms character most readily, children must not hear casual tales, and a censorship of writers of fiction must accept good tales and reject bad ones for mothers and nurses to use, discarding most tales now in circulation.

nodes.speaker: Socrates with Adeimantus; embedded sidenotes give editorial headings

nodes.label: God is good, changeless, true
nodes.summary: Modelled on the truths of the framed laws, poets must represent God as truly is: since God is good and the good does no evil and is the cause of well-being, God is the author only of good, so the causes of human evils must be sought elsewhere (though just punishment may be attributed to God). Further, things at their best are least altered, so God neither takes many shapes nor changes himself, and — the true lie being ignorance of highest matters in the soul, its verbal form only an imitation — no motive or need for deception could apply to God, who is simple and true in word and deed; poets' tales asserting the contrary are to be barred from the State and from teaching.

evidence.rationale: An argument linking premises about God's goodness, perfection and truth to explicit limits on poetry. X follows primary theme “Forming character by nurture: music, gymnastics, restricted stories, and the limits of law”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Underworld tales banished
nodes.summary: Since belief in a real and terrible world below destroys courage, narrators must commend rather than revile it; Homer's verses on gloomy Hades, mindless shades and shrieking souls are to be struck out—its poetical charm makes them more unfit for free men, who should fear slavery more than death—and terrifying names such as Cocytus and Styx are likewise dropped in favour of a nobler strain.

nodes.speaker: Socrates, with Adeimantus assenting

nodes.label: Lament for the dead banished
nodes.summary: From the principle that the good man does not fear death for a good comrade, is sufficient for himself, and so feels loss least, weepings of famous men are to be assigned to women or baser men; Homer must not show Achilles or Priam rolling in the dirt and wailing, still less the gods lamenting, since youths who take such scenes seriously, instead of laughing at them, lose shame and self-control and whine on slight occasions.

X follows primary theme “Forming character by nurture: music, gymnastics, restricted stories, and the limits of law”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. nodes.speaker: Socrates, with Adeimantus assenting

nodes.label: Lying as rulers' medicine
nodes.summary: Truth is highly valued: a lie is useless to the gods and, like medicine, belongs to the physician—here the rulers, who alone may lie for the public good against enemies or citizens; any other liar in the state, whether priest, physician or carpenter, is a fault worse than a patient hiding his illness from his doctor, and is to be punished as one who subverts ship or state.

nodes.label: Crimes of heroes rejected
nodes.summary: Socrates declines to believe Achilles took gifts, ransomed Hector's body for pay, defied Apollo and the river-god, and slaughtered captives, and refuses the tales of Theseus and Peirithous' violent rape: poets must declare either that these deeds were not done or that their doers were not sons of gods—not both at once—lest hearers excuse their own vices by the example of god-born kin and morals loosen among the young.

nodes.label: Justice first, then human praise
nodes.summary: Socrates says the further question—what poets may say about men—cannot be settled now: their claims that the wicked are often happy, injustice profitable when undetected, and justice a man's own loss are to be forbidden and the opposite sung, but whether such things may be said awaits the discovery of what justice is and how it benefits its possessor, whether he seems just or not.

nodes.label: Narration, imitation, or mixture
nodes.summary: Poetry and myth narrate events, but narration may be simple, imitative, or mixed: the poet imitates when he assimilates himself to another's voice and gesture (as Homer takes Chryses' part after the opening lines of the Iliad) and drops into simple narration when he speaks throughout in his own person; tragedy and comedy are wholly imitative, the dithyramb purely narrative, epic and some other kinds a combination.

nodes.speaker: Socrates, with Adeimantus answering

nodes.label: Guardians' imitation confined
nodes.summary: Since one man can do only one thing well, guardians may not imitate many parts: imitation continued from youth becomes a second nature in body, voice and mind, so they may imitate only suitable characters—the courageous, temperate, holy, free and the like—and not women in distress, slaves, cowards, madmen or craftsmen; the good man's style mixes much narration with little imitation, and the versatile pantomimic poet is honoured and garlanded but sent to another city.

evidence.rationale: A reusable norm of practice—each person one craft and imitation fixing second nature—that organizes the rules of guardians' performance and the exile of particular poets. nodes.summary: Physicians may know disease from their own bodies, since they cure body by mind; judges govern mind by mind and so must be old, uncorrupted in youth, and taught of vice only by long observation of others, for vice cannot know virtue while a virtuous nature knows both.

nodes.summary: Guardians are to live like soldiers in a camp: no private property, houses or stores, only fixed yearly provisions from the citizens for trained, temperate warriors, and gold and silver forbidden to them; failure of these rules, the passage argues, turns guardians into husbandmen, tyrants and enemies who fear their fellow citizens more than foreign foes and bring ruin to the State.

nodes.label: Happiness of the whole city
nodes.summary: Socrates answers that the guardians may in fact be the happiest of men, but the state is founded for the happiness of the whole, not of one class; like a statue, each feature must keep its proportion rather than be beautified out of its function. nodes.summary: Socrates claims two causes degrade the arts: wealth makes the potter indolent and careless; poverty leaves him without tools and unable to work or teach his sons and apprentices. nodes.summary: Socrates says the earlier regulations are trifles as long as the one thing is cared for: education and nurture. nodes.summary: Socrates describes present students of philosophy as beginning near childhood, giving it only time spared from moneymaking and housekeeping, and abandoning dialectic at its difficulty until in old age they go out like a sun that never relights. nodes.sourceLabel: BOOK VIII · dialogue · Socrates ('I said')
nodes.speaker: Socrates ('I said')

nodes.label: Making of the tyrannical man
nodes.summary: Socrates recounts how the democratic man's son is drawn into a lawless life his seducers call 'perfect liberty'; when the 'tyrant-makers' lose hold, they implant a master passion — imaged as a monstrous winged drone — to lord over his idle lusts. Nourished by his other lusts, this ruler breaks out with Madness as captain of the guard, extinguishing remaining shame and good opinions and purging temperance. On this account Love is rightly called a tyrant; drunkenness and derangement show the same spirit, and the tyrannical man arises when nature or habit makes him drunken, lustful, passionate. nodes.summary: Socrates asserts that money- and honour-lovers who pursue their proper pleasures under reason and knowledge attain the truest pleasures available to their nature, and that when the whole soul follows the philosophical principle each part does its own work and enjoys its best pleasure; the further a part is from reason, the more illusive its pleasure.

nodes.label: Tyrant 729 times from king
nodes.summary: Socrates proposes one genuine and two spurious pleasures and places the tyrant three remove from the oligarch and the oligarch three from the royal type, so that in the completed solid calculation the king lives 729 times more pleasantly than the tyrant — a number relevant to human life per the dialogue, with an editorial footnote noting 729 nearly equals the year's days and nights.

X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Editor on dialectic and eristic
nodes.summary: A bracketed editor's note treats dialectic as the coping stone of knowledge, distinguished from eristic, and as employing scientific hypotheses as steps toward ideas and truth; the note concedes this conception was probably no clearer to Plato himself (referring to the Introduction), finds it firmer as analysis plus synthesis in Sophist and Statesman, and says the Laws demotes dialectic to question-and-answer discussion (7.820 C; 10.891).

nodes.label: Editor on two-part education
nodes.summary: A bracketed editor's note divides the Republic's education into (1) common Hellenic music and gymnastic — both ultimately for the soul, music (including literature) preceding gymnastic, shared by boys and girls, with fiction censored and fair surroundings essential — and (2) the rulers' special education: selection at twenty, ten years of arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and harmony pursued non-utilistically and combined through dialectic, five years of philosophy at thirty, fifteen years of public life, then philosophy again after fifty.

nodes.label: Editorial: God across Republic/Laws
nodes.summary: Editorial note summing up the Republic's theology under two heads—God is perfect and unchangeable, and God is true and the author of truth—and presenting these as the canons by which poetry is judged. The editor adds that Plato later hardens (Laws) but repeats many Republic theses (God is not the author of evil, will not favor the unjust), and that the Demiurge of Timaeus, Sophist and Statesman hardly appears in Republic or Laws.

nodes.summary: Editorial note maintaining that the Idea of Good as named is an abstraction not otherwise found in Plato, probably akin to 'the true being of things', and that Plato never explained his meaning precisely. The editor suggests Plato valued abstractions above facts yet used the cave allegory to demand a firm starting point, and offers Philebus 65 A (Beauty, Symmetry, Truth) as the best insight into the ideal of perfection.

nodes.label: Editorial: justice frames Republic
nodes.summary: Editorial note presenting the search for justice as the foundation of the Republic: First Book definitions fail, Glaucon and Adeimantus demand proof justice is a good in itself (I have placed them as speakers of their own reported challenges), and Socrates proposes the state-in-larger-letters so justice appears as the bond of social organization and the principle that each do his own work. The proof runs through the decline from ideal to actual constitutions, culminating in the tyrant's '729 times less pleasure' than the king's, and extends to rewards after death.

nodes.label: Music in the wide sense
nodes.summary: Editorial commentary states that Greek 'music' meant mental training opposed to gymnastic, spanning reading and writing, mathematics, harmony and poetry (drawing being sometimes a separate division, per Aristotle). It says Plato places music before gymnastic and treats strictly musical education as shaping harmonious character and true conceptions of good and evil rather than idle pleasure or virtuoso performance.

nodes.label: Against novelty in music
nodes.summary: The editor states that Plato's simplicity and fixity in music (restricted instruments and modes, no change in musical fashion) probably opposed the ornate tendencies of his own age, and that Plato treated that change as a cause rather than a sign of Hellas' decline. The editor dissents from Plato's view, judging the change 'inevitable, and not perhaps wholly to be regretted' — an explicit editorial difference from the author it describes.

evidence.rationale: A historical and evaluative claim about Plato's position and its context. X follows primary theme “Forming character by nurture: music, gymnastics, restricted stories, and the limits of law”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. nodes.speaker: editor (bracketed index commentary)

nodes.label: The case against poetry
nodes.summary: Editorial essay presenting the Republic as Plato's first serious examination of poetry's place in education and the state. It traces a two-stage argument: in Books II–III the epic and tragic tales are tested for truth and fitness, and objectionable passages are to be expunged under censorship; in Book X the charge deepens — the poet is an impostor thrice removed from truth whose imitations supply corrupt models — ending in banishment unless 'the lovers of poetry' answer the charges. The essay sets this beside the Laws, where the poet is tolerated only in harmony with the laws.

evidence.rationale: An argument organizing several concepts: poetic truth, censorship, imitation, and exile of the poets. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.speaker: editor (bracketed index commentary)

nodes.label: Tripartite and fourfold soul
nodes.summary: Editorial essay describing the Republic's psychology as both continuous with and a development of the other dialogues: the division into reason, spirit and appetite here 'first assumes a precise form', underlies the classification of governments, and makes virtue the harmony of the elements (reason enforced by passion against appetite) and vice their anarchy. On the intellectual side the editor counts four faculties answering to four divisions of knowledge and the Platonic 'proportion', while judging these divisions 'partly real, partly formed by a logical process, which... has outrun fact' and pointing to the cave as illustration.

evidence.rationale: An argument organizing several concepts: parts of soul, virtue as harmony, faculties of knowledge. X follows primary theme “From sight to being: the philosopher, the ascent, and the idea of Good as the summit of education”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Immortality and Er's myth
nodes.summary: Editorial claims that pre-existence and immortality are assumed rather than proved here (recollection being at most glanced at in Er's water of Unmindfulness), and that the immortality argument is 'chiefly of a verbal character' and less emphatic than the Phaedo's. It reads Er's narrative as the favoured mythic vehicle for rewards, punishments and the choice of lives, with the philosopher's wisdom securing a good choice rather than release from embodiment, and suggests the transmigration doctrine came via Pythagorean channels from an Oriental source but 'probably had a real hold on his mind'.

evidence.rationale: Claims about the argument's force and the myth's function and provenance. X follows primary theme “Poetry versus philosophy, the immortal soul's fate, and the afterlife of ideal states”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Republic's state: two mixed elements
nodes.summary: Editor's index commentary argues that the polity Plato sketches in the Republic combines two elements — an older Hellenic, partly Spartan-type state (small citizen body, subordination of individual to state, war as normal condition) and an ideal city of common possessions ruled by philosopher-rulers chosen by merit — and that, as Aristotle complained, the two are not perfectly combined and much is left ill-defined.

evidence.rationale: An editorial argument organising several concepts (state size, civic subordination, common property, women, philosopher rule). X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Whole's happiness secures the parts
nodes.summary: The editor reports that when Adeimantus objects to the citizens' harsh garrison-like life (Republic 4. 419), Socrates answers that if the happiness of the whole is secured the happiness of the parts follows; this is cited as one mark of the older Hellenic element, with the individual subordinated to the state.

evidence.rationale: A claim about the state–individual relation, reported second-hand by the editor. nodes.label: Three peculiar institutions
nodes.summary: The editor singles out three features as most peculiar to Plato's state: community of property (paralleled at most by Sparta, Crete, or the Pythagorean brotherhood), the position of women, and government by philosophers.

evidence.rationale: A bounded claim enumerating the distinctive traits of the second element. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.speaker: index editor (editorial commentary)

nodes.label: Women's place vs Hellenic custom
nodes.summary: The editor judges that nothing in the Republic would have struck contemporaries more than Plato's assignment to women of common marriage, equal education, war service, and administration — worse to Athenian eyes than the reputed licence of Spartan women, whose public influence was indirect and who held no office or arms, while upper-class Athenian women lived in seclusion. The index entry 'Women' gathers the corresponding loci (training like men, gymnasium, war, guardianship, common wives and children) and points back to this State article.

evidence.rationale: A comparative claim contrasting Plato's arrangements with Spartan and Athenian practice. X follows primary theme “The guardian paradoxes: shared duties, community of women, children, and goods”; Z derives from the first exact passage offset. Classification is a model interpretation.

nodes.label: Decline of regimes into tyranny
nodes.summary: The index entries 'Timocracy', 'Tyranny', and 'Tyrant, the' sketch a descent: timocracy's origin in Republic 8. 545 foll., tyranny as injustice on the grand scale and the wretchedest government, the tyrant's rise, taxes, army, purgation of the city, his misery, lack of friends or real pleasure, and his posthumous punishment.

edges.rationale: The justice-search in which justice vanishes in the individual and reappears in the ideal State is the concrete itinerary of the claim that justice is the order of the State.
The finding of two really opposed points of view and an imperfect whole provides grounds for the warning against expecting one design.
The stress on many designs and on the work's poetic, non-logical character objects to the clean claim that justice and State blend in one as the writer's single intention.
Thrasymachus prohibits the ordinary definitions of justice and replaces them with his own answer (
Glaucon is dissatisfied with Socrates' indirect disposal of the question whether the just or the unjust are happier and presses for a direct proof.
The State-first, indirect answer grounds the claim that justice is enlarged into order in the State and then the individual.
The remark on State-before-individual refines and qualifies the State-first ordering asserted in the answer.
Building the city to read justice in its larger letters is the concrete instance of the prescribed State-then-individual method.
The censorship of tales extends the guardianship episode into the education its closing question demands.
Regulating narrative kind and imitation extends the poetic censorship of tales to the manner of telling.
The note questions the claim that judges must know vice only from observation, citing evidence to the contrary.

the later passage extends the duty/happiness question by ranking right and truth above happiness in ethics and politics.
the commentary objects that the residue-method cannot cleanly separate justice from temperance.
the tripartite-soul argument grounds applying the city's own-work definition of justice to the individual.

the second wave extends the first wave's admission of shared duties to community of wives and children.

The account of knowledge and opinion supplies what a true philosopher—needed for the proposed rule—is.
The editor argues the kinship prohibitions and lot arrangements of the marriage scheme cannot work as stated.
The editor rejects the 'contingent matter' doctrine as a confusion of the contingent with the relative and of degrees of knowledge with degrees of being.
Adeimantus's report that philosophers turn out rogues or fools is set against the claim that philosophers should rule.
The diagnosis of how good natures are corrupted by environment and public opinion provides grounds for the observed outcome.
The guardians as rulers are carried further: they must be philosophers and ascend to knowledge of the good.
The divided line extends the sun analogy of 508–509 into a graded scheme whose top is the idea of good.
The admitted infirmity of the long interrogative argument motivates the move to a positive, constructive method.
The commentator denies that 'corruptio optimi pessima' holds generally of the best natures.
The envisaged higher method refines the intelligible ascent of the divided line into a self-supporting whole of ideas.
The cave parable narrativizes the line's grades (shadows to sun) and adds the political theme of compelled return.
The three-fingers and great-small cases instantiate number's role in turning the mind to being.
Abstract number is presented as the first stage that lifts the mind toward being and the good.
Geometry's upward study of true being belongs to the prelude preparing dialectic.
The sciences in their natural relation to one another and the good are explicitly called the prelude to dialectic.
Dialectic is the coping-stone training required of the future rulers whose selection is then prescribed.
The warning against early dialectic refines the age staging of the ruler-training program.
The Muses' account of decay is the first stage of the constitution–character sequence framed in node 0.
The split of the metal races and their compromise on private property supplies grounds for timocracy's emergence.
The timocratic state and man instantiate and refine the state-then-individual parallel.
Oligarchy extends the decline: hoarded gold and silver make lovers of money displace lovers of honour.
Democracy extends the sequence when oligarchic avarice and debt ruin produces the poor's victory over the rich.
Tyranny is carried further out of democracy's excess of freedom and lawlessness.
The genuine-versus-apparent pleasure distinction grounds the claim that the philosopher's rational pleasure is truest.
The beast–lion–man image concretises the three-part soul presupposed by the three pleasure-types.
Argues that inferring a pleasure's unreality from its transience, and intellectual pleasures' durability from knowledge, are illusions.
The doctrine that the imitator is thrice removed and without knowledge is extended into the claim that imitation serves the inferior part of the soul.
The charge that poetry enfeebles reason and feeds the passions is expressly given as the ground for the prohibition and its terms.
The elevation of universals over sense-particulars gives the metaphysical ground for the charge that imitation addresses the lower, emotional faculties.
Denies the essential truth of universals over particulars on which the poetry/philosophy split is built.
Contests the charge that emotional expression is harmful, holding feelings to be neutral and art to enlist feeling on the side of reason.
Extends the claim that art can embody the highest truth into a proposed ideal poetry and a question about its public use.
Community of goods is identified as the first of the paradoxes introduced.
Community of wives and children is named as the second paradox of the perfect State.

The closing argument extends the moral-over-physical critique by denying that breeding can procure human excellence.
The claim that family illness can be foreseen and prevented grounds the prudential restraint of marriage urged in the population argument.

Calling Plato's state-as-one-man analogy partly fallacious undermines the conceptual basis of the all-sufficing State.
The dialectic-and-the-good account extends the mathematics-as-abstraction account to a higher grade of knowledge.

Making education continue through life refines and extends the staged scheme of which mathematical abstraction is the second stage.
Dante's vision of future government, confessedly bound up with the beliefs of his own age, is an instance of the ideals that remain 'visions of a world unrealized'.

The fallible-ruler objection turns Thrasymachus's definition into its opposite.
Showing that harming produces injustice refutes the good-to-friends/harm-to-enemies definition.
Thrasymachus dismisses the Socrates-Polemarchus exchange and substitutes his own definition.

Justice as the soul's excellence underwrites the step from living well to happiness.
The happiness of the just, with happiness as profitable, grounds the conclusion on relative profitability.
